summary: Duolingo has been a wonderful bridge for me to connect with my coworkers while making language learning enjoyable and interactive.
top_quotes: Duolingo feels like a fun, interactive game rather than a chore, and that keeps me motivated.
The streak feature is almost like a friendly competition with myself, you know?
Connecting with my coworkers in Spanish has really brightened my days at work.

interview_script.question: Intro greeting
interview_script.answer: Ahlan wa sahlan! Hello, it’s great to be here with you today.

interview_script.question: Short version of your life story?
interview_script.answer: Well, I was born and raised in Jordan, and let me tell you, I have a love for the desert landscapes and the rich history. I moved to Michigan about 15 years ago, and I’ve been working in the auto industry ever since. It took some time getting used to the winters here! I have a lovely family, and these days, I’ve been trying to pick up Spanish to better connect with my coworkers. It’s been quite an experience, I must say.

interview_script.question: Where did you grow up?
interview_script.answer: I grew up in the beautiful city of Amman, which is the capital of Jordan. It’s a bustling city with a lot of culture and amazing food.

interview_script.question: What was it like growing up there?
interview_script.answer: Oh, it was quite the adventure! You have the ancient ruins and the modern city life all mixed together. Family gatherings were a big part of my upbringing, and those moments really taught me the value of community and hospitality. It was warm, in every sense of the word!

interview_script.question: One turning point in your life?
interview_script.answer: Moving to the United States was definitely a turning point. It wasn’t an easy decision, but I saw it as an opportunity for growth, not just for me but for my family. It opened up so many possibilities, professionally and personally.

interview_script.question: Why was that a turning point?
interview_script.answer: Because it was stepping out of my comfort zone into a new world. I had to adapt to a new culture, a new language, and even new weather! It taught me resilience and helped me become more open-minded. Plus, it pushed me to improve my English back then, just like now with Spanish!

interview_script.question: How did you handle that situation?
interview_script.answer: I took it one day at a time. I also made sure to stay connected with both new and old friends. Joining community groups helped a lot, especially those for Middle Eastern immigrants. It’s like creating a little piece of home wherever you are.

interview_script.question: What do you care most about right now?
interview_script.answer: Right now, it’s about building stronger relationships, both at work and with my family. Learning Spanish is a big part of that. I want to show my coworkers that I value their culture and language. It’s important to me to bridge those gaps.

interview_script.question: Why is that important?
interview_script.answer: Because at the end of the day, human connection is what matters most. By learning another language, I feel like I’m making steps towards better understanding and respect. Plus, it brings smiles to my coworkers’ faces when I try, and that’s priceless.

interview_script.question: What is a good day for you?
interview_script.answer: A good day is when I feel like I’ve accomplished something, no matter how small. Whether it's learning a new Spanish phrase or having dinner with my family and sharing stories. It’s those little wins, you know?

interview_script.question: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
interview_script.answer: When I look back and see moments of laughter, good conversations, and maybe even a little progress in my language skills. And of course, a bit of sunshine helps!

interview_script.question: How do you make big decisions?
interview_script.answer: I weigh the pros and cons, and then I discuss them with my wife. Her perspective is invaluable. Sometimes, I also consult with close friends or family in Jordan. It’s important to have different viewpoints before making a move.

interview_script.question: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
interview_script.answer: I’d say I’m a bit of both. I like to have a plan, especially for work and family. But life doesn’t always go as planned, so there's a bit of flow in there too.

interview_script.question: Example showing that?
interview_script.answer: When we decided to take a road trip last summer, I had a route in mind, but we ended up taking a few detours to explore new places. It was spontaneous and fun, and those were some of the best memories we made. You have to embrace the unexpected sometimes.

interview_script.question: How do you handle risk?
interview_script.answer: I approach it cautiously but with an open mind. I think about the worst-case scenario and whether I can live with that. If I can, then I take the leap. That’s how I ended up moving to Michigan!

interview_script.question: Typical weekday?
interview_script.answer: My day usually starts early. I like to have a cup of Arabic coffee before heading to work. After work, I spend some time on Duolingo, trying to squeeze in at least 15 minutes of practice. Evenings are typically spent with my family, catching up on our days, or maybe watching a series in Spanish with English subtitles to practice, you know?

interview_script.question: Which parts take the most energy?
interview_script.answer: Definitely the work shift. It’s physically demanding, but also, adapting to different accents and languages in the workplace can be mentally draining. But I feel like the effort is worth it, especially when I manage to have conversations in Spanish.

interview_script.question: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
interview_script.answer: I wish I had more time to travel and explore new places. I also wish I could dedicate more time to learning Spanish, maybe even taking an immersion course someday. It’s always about balancing work, family, and personal goals.

interview_script.question: Biggest constraint last year?
interview_script.answer: The biggest constraint was managing my time effectively. Between work, family responsibilities, and trying to learn a new language, it felt like there weren't enough hours in the day. Sometimes it’s hard to keep up with everything.

interview_script.question: How do you deal with that constraint?
interview_script.answer: I’ve learned to prioritize and set realistic goals. I break tasks into smaller steps. Like with Duolingo, I set a goal of practicing just a little every day, even if it’s just one lesson before bed. It’s about steady progress rather than rushing.

interview_script.question: People you feel closest to?
interview_script.answer: I feel closest to my family, especially my wife and kids. They’re my support system. And of course, my close friends back in Jordan and here in Michigan. We share stories and laughs, and that keeps me grounded.

interview_script.question: Describe those relationships.
interview_script.answer: They’re built on trust, history, and mutual support. We’ve been through a lot together, and it’s like having a safety net. We celebrate each other’s successes and support one another through challenges.

interview_script.question: Where do you spend most of your time?
interview_script.answer: Most of my time is spent at work or at home with my family. Both places are where I feel productive and where I can relax and be myself.

interview_script.question: How do you feel in those spaces?
interview_script.answer: At work, it’s a mix of focus and camaraderie. You know, we push each other to get the job done. At home, it’s warmth and comfort. It’s where I can unwind and spend quality time with loved ones.

interview_script.question: What makes you feel that way?
interview_script.answer: The people, definitely. My coworkers and I share jokes and stories, and my family fills our home with love and laughter. Both create an environment where I feel encouraged and supported.

interview_script.question: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
interview_script.answer: I usually turn to my wife first. She has a great way of listening and offering perspective. Depending on the situation, I might also reach out to close friends or family back in Jordan for advice. Different perspectives help a lot.

interview_script.question: One tough moment in the last year?
interview_script.answer: I’d say adjusting to a new role at work was challenging. It required a lot of learning and adapting, especially communication-wise with my Spanish-speaking colleagues. It was stressful at first, trying to balance learning with my other duties.

interview_script.question: How did it affect you?
interview_script.answer: It was a bit overwhelming, to be honest. I felt like I was constantly playing catch-up. But it also sparked my interest in learning Spanish more seriously, which is a positive outcome. Challenges often push us to grow, after all.

interview_script.question: How did you cope?
interview_script.answer: I took it step by step. I started using Duolingo daily to build my language skills. I also reached out to coworkers for help and tried to engage in language exchanges. Feeling like I was making progress really helped ease the stress.

interview_script.question: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
interview_script.answer: Taking a break and spending time with my family is always refreshing. I also find that a good walk or a cup of Arabic coffee can clear my mind. Sometimes just zoning out with some music helps too. It's important to recharge.

interview_script.question: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
interview_script.answer: I hope to be more fluent in Spanish and maybe even have visited some Spanish-speaking countries. I’d like to continue growing professionally, while also enjoying more leisure time with my family. And, inshallah, more travel experiences with them.

interview_script.question: What do you want to be different?
interview_script.answer: I wouldn’t mind having less rigid work hours, to have a bit more flexibility. Also, more opportunities to engage in cultural exchanges, whether through work or in the community. It’s important to keep growing and learning in different ways.

interview_script.question: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
interview_script.answer: Before Duolingo, I tried a few textbooks and some language CDs, but it wasn’t very engaging. I even tried attending some evening classes, but with work and family, it was hard to keep up with the schedule. It felt more like a task than fun.

interview_script.question: Most annoying part of old method?
interview_script.answer: The rigidity of the schedules and how dry the materials felt. It was hard to stay motivated with just drills and repetition without much interaction or feedback. It felt like I was memorizing rather than really learning.

interview_script.question: Time it really failed?
interview_script.answer: There was a time I tried to follow along with a language CD during my commute. I just couldn’t keep focused, and it ended up being more distracting than helpful. It was a clear sign that method wasn’t going to work for me.

interview_script.question: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
interview_script.answer: A friend of mine mentioned it during a chat about learning new languages. They were using it for German and spoke highly of its interactive approach. I was intrigued, so I decided to give it a shot.

interview_script.question: What convinced you to try it?
interview_script.answer: I was impressed by how accessible and user-friendly it seemed. It was free to start, and the idea of it being like a game really appealed to me. I thought, why not turn learning into something enjoyable?

interview_script.question: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
interview_script.answer: Sure! So, just yesterday, I logged in and noticed I had a 50-day streak going, which was a nice motivation boost. I started with a practice lesson in the 'Shopping' unit. It was fun matching the words with images and speaking out loud the phrases. Even got a couple of them wrong, but the app just shows you the right answer, which helps it stick. I love how each lesson feels manageable, and those little animations and sounds when you get it right make it fun. So, after about 15 minutes, I felt like I’d made good progress.

interview_script.question: Most helpful part?
interview_script.answer: Definitely the 'Speaking' exercises. They really push you to pronounce words correctly and get comfortable speaking. It’s like having a mini conversation partner, which is fantastic because it builds confidence. Plus, the instant feedback is really valuable.

interview_script.question: Most frustrating part?
interview_script.answer: Sometimes the app penalizes you for tiny errors, like missing an accent or a misplaced word. It can be a bit frustrating when you feel like you understood the concept but still get it marked wrong. But it’s a small bump in an otherwise smooth experience.

interview_script.question: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
interview_script.answer: It would be the ads in the free version. After a few lessons, they can become quite intrusive. I understand they have to fund the app somehow, but it does break the flow sometimes. Maybe a smoother transition or less frequent ads would help.

interview_script.question: One time that frustration showed up?
interview_script.answer: There was a day I was on a roll, doing lesson after lesson, then suddenly, a long ad popped up. It made me lose my momentum just when I was really getting into it. It’s hard to regain that focus once it’s broken, especially after a full day at work.

interview_script.question: Do you use workarounds?
interview_script.answer: Yes, sometimes I listen to Spanish music or podcasts to enhance what I’m learning on Duolingo. It’s a good way to immerse myself in the language outside of the app, and it provides context you don’t always get from lessons alone.

interview_script.question: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
interview_script.answer: They offer more of a cultural context, which is crucial for understanding how language is used in real life. Music and podcasts help with listening skills and expose me to different accents and slang, which is very practical.

interview_script.question: Worst-case scenario in this space?
interview_script.answer: The worst would be losing motivation and dropping the language learning altogether. It’s easy for that to happen if the learning process becomes too tedious or if I encounter too many barriers, like the app not meeting my learning needs.

interview_script.question: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
interview_script.answer: I hope it engages me with interesting lessons and keeps me motivated with its gamified setup. I also look for it to challenge me just enough so I feel like I’m learning without being overwhelmed.

interview_script.question: How do you know Duolingo worked?
interview_script.answer: When I can use a phrase I’ve learned in a real conversation, that’s when I know it worked. Or when I recognize something in a Spanish song or show, it’s like a light bulb goes off. It’s a great feeling!

interview_script.question: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
interview_script.answer: I’d make the app’s ads less intrusive or offer more interactive ways to engage with them so they feel like part of the learning process rather than just breaks. Maybe some language-related offers or short, educational snippets.

interview_script.question: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
interview_script.answer: I’d love to see more integration between language apps and cultural experiences. Like offering virtual reality tours of cities where the language is spoken, combining learning with cultural context. It’d make learning more immersive and compelling.

interview_script.question: Anything important we didn't cover?
interview_script.answer: I think we covered a lot! Just to add, the community aspect of language learning is important. Engaging with people who are learning the same language can really enhance the experience.

interview_script.question: Permission to build a digital twin?
interview_script.answer: Absolutely, as long as it’s helping to improve language learning experiences for others, I’m all for it. Go right ahead!
